hints: Work out the oxidation number of Cl in $\text{HCl}$ and in $\text{Cl}_2$, then decide if it has increased or decreased.
walkthrough:
Track what happens to chlorine**
Think of an oxidising agent as something that takes electrons from another species and oxidises it. In $\text{HCl}$, Cl is $\text{Cl}^-$ with oxidation number -1. In $\text{Cl}_2$, each Cl is 0. So chlorine has lost electrons, it has been oxidised.

Link this to $\text{MnO}_2$**
Because $\text{MnO}_2$ causes this oxidation of $\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{Cl}_2$ (while Mn itself is reduced from +4 to +2), it is acting as the oxidising agent.
Final answer: It oxidises chloride ions from oxidation number -1 in $\text{HCl}$ to 0 in $\text{Cl}_2$.

hints: Look at the state symbols in the equation to see which products would give visible bubbling or colour.
walkthrough:
Picture the reaction mixture**
You start with black solid $\text{MnO}_2$ in colourless $\text{HCl(aq)}$. The equation shows a gas $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$ is made, so picture bubbles rising through the liquid.

Add colour and solid change**
Chlorine is a pale green gas, so you would see effervescence and a green gas. The black solid also dissolves as it reacts to form soluble $\text{MnCl}_2\text{(aq)}$.
Final answer: Effervescence / bubbling due to formation of pale green $\text{Cl}_2$ gas (and black solid $\text{MnO}_2$ dissolves).

hints: Recall whether chlorine, bromine and iodine are gases, liquids or solids at room temperature to decide if volatility increases or decreases down the group.
Identify the only intermolecular force between non-polar $\text{X}_2$ molecules that has to be overcome on boiling.
Think how the number of electrons per molecule changes from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$ and how this affects temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
Translate volatility into boiling**
Volatility means how easily a liquid turns to vapour. Chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid at room temperature. That shows it gets harder to vaporise going down, so volatility decreases and boiling point increases.

See what must be broken**
Halogens are simple covalent $\text{X}_2$ molecules. When they boil you do not break the strong $\text{X-X}$ covalent bond, you only separate molecules from each other. The only attraction to overcome is London dispersion forces, the instantaneous induced dipole-dipole forces.

Explain why the forces get stronger**
Going down from $\text{Cl}_2$ (34 electrons) to $\text{Br}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$ (106 electrons), each molecule has many more electrons and a larger, more easily distorted electron cloud. This gives larger temporary dipoles and stronger induced attractions between molecules.

Connect to energy**
Stronger intermolecular forces need more thermal energy to break apart, so boiling point rises and volatility falls down Group 17.

Final answer: Volatility decreases down Group 17.
Down the group there is a greater number of electrons per molecule, giving stronger instantaneous induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion) forces.
More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so boiling point increases.

hints: Recall the three products formed when $\text{Cl}_2$ reacts with cold dilute $\text{NaOH}$: a chloride, a chlorate(I) and water.
Assign the oxidation number of Cl in $\text{Cl}_2$ and in the two chlorine-containing products to show both oxidation and reduction of the same element.
walkthrough:
Write the cold alkali equation**
With cold aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, chlorine gives sodium chloride, sodium chlorate(I), $\text{NaClO}$, and water. Balance it as: $$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Show simultaneous oxidation and reduction**
Disproportionation means the same element is both oxidised and reduced. Here $\text{Cl}_2$ starts at 0. In $\text{NaCl}$, Cl is -1 (reduction, gain of electrons). In $\text{NaClO}$, Cl is +1 (oxidation, loss of electrons). One $\text{Cl}_2$ does both, so this fits perfectly.

Final answer: Equation: $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
Chlorine is both oxidised (0 to +1 in $\text{NaClO}$) and reduced (0 to -1 in $\text{NaCl}$), so it is disproportionation.

hints: Remember that hot concentrated alkali oxidises chlorine further than cold alkali, giving chlorate(V) with oxidation number +5 instead of +1.
walkthrough:
Spot the hot condition difference**
With hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ the reaction is: $$3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The chlorate(I) product $\text{NaClO}$ is replaced by chlorate(V), $\text{NaClO}_3$, where Cl is +5.
Final answer: $\text{NaClO}_3$ / sodium chlorate(V)

hints: Think what chlorine forms when it reacts with water, and which of those products is the active disinfectant.
Consider why drinking water must be treated biologically, linking the chemical to killing microbes.
walkthrough:
Form the active chemical**
When $\text{Cl}_2$ is added to water it forms $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HClO}$: $$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HCl} + \text{HClO}$$ The useful product is chloric(I) acid, $\text{HClO}$.

Explain its killing action**
$\text{HClO}$ is a strong oxidising disinfectant. It kills bacteria and other pathogens in the water, making the water safe to drink. That is why chlorine is added in water treatment.

Final answer: Chlorine reacts with water to form chloric(I) acid / hypochlorous acid, $\text{HClO}$.
$\text{HClO}$ kills bacteria / micro-organisms, sterilising drinking water.

hints: Recall what type of energy is needed to split $\text{Cl-Cl}$ homolytically to start a radical chain.
walkthrough:
Start the radical chain**
Free-radical substitution needs $\text{Cl}$ radicals first. The $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond is broken homolytically by high energy light: $$\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{uv} 2\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$$ So ultraviolet light or sunlight is required to initiate the reaction.
Final answer: Ultraviolet light / sunlight

hints: Remember that in overall free-radical substitution one H in the alkane is replaced by Cl, with $\text{HCl}$ as the second product.
walkthrough:
Write the overall change**
Do not write the radical steps here, only the overall stoichiometry. One hydrogen of ethane is substituted by chlorine: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$ Check atoms balance: 2 C, 6 H and 2 Cl on each side.
